quote: (1.7)(c) ... with respect to taxable years commencing on or after January 1, 2022, a tax of four and forty one-hundredths percent is imposed on the federal taxable income
notes: Colorado has a single flat rate (4.40% for 2022 onward, subject to the separate TABOR temporary-reduction mechanism in 39-22-627); there are no bracket thresholds, so the only band start (0) cannot be indexed. Source is the 2024 Colorado Revised Statutes printout (Title 39 PDF).

quote: Amounts subtracted under this subsection (4)(f) are capped at twenty thousand dollars per tax year for any individual who is fifty-five years of age or older but less than sixty-five... capped at twenty-four thousand dollars per tax year for any individual who is sixty-five years of age or older
section: C.R.S. 39-22-104(4)(f)(III)(A),(B); military: 39-22-104(4)(y)(I)(D) 'Fifteen thousand dollars for income tax years commencing on or after January 1, 2022, but before January 1, 2029'
notes: Fixed dollar amounts, no inflation language in (4)(f) or (4)(y) of the 2024 C.R.S. A 2024 interim-committee draft (Bill 7, LLS 25-0221) and SB25-136 proposed changes (the draft would index caps to the Denver-Aurora-Lakewood CPI) but those are bills; I did not confirm enactment of anything touching (4)(f) after 2024 (SB25-136 as introduced removed the caps from 2026). Re-check the current-year statute if the dataset covers years after 2025. The military cap also sunsets (tax years before 2029) - fixed, not indexed. The SS-related increase of the cap to the amount of SS benefits is a floor tied to actual benefits, not an indexation.
